Key observations from the test image:
- Soybean plant pulled from soil showing stem cross-section and root system
- **White/cream pith** visible in the split stem
- Severely rotted, blackened root system with dead lateral roots
- Stem exterior appears tan/light colored

The white pith + rotted roots strongly points toward **Sudden Death Syndrome** (SDS distinguishes from Brown Stem Rot by pith remaining white). Let me confirm with reference images.
The Fusarium reference images look very similar to the test image — white pith, blackened rotted roots. Let me compare with Phytophthora and Rhizoctonia, and get a closer look at SDS.
The Fusarium reference is very close to the test image. Let me also check a few more references to be thorough.

Now I have enough reference images to make my decision. Let me analyze the evidence:

**Test image key features:**
- Mature soybean plant pulled from soil, held horizontally
- Stem split longitudinally showing **white/cream pith** throughout
- Severely rotted, **completely blackened root system** — lateral roots dead and black
- Stem exterior: tan/light colored
- No blue fungal growth visible, no chocolate-brown stem discoloration

**Ruling out:**
- **Brown Stem Rot**: pith would be brown (reference confirmed brown interior)
- **Phytophthora**: chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending upward (not present)
- **Rhizoctonia**: reddish-brown hypocotyl lesions, seedling stage
- **Pythium**: seedling damping off with water-soaked lesions
- **Charcoal Rot**: gray/marbled internal tissue with microsclerotia (not white)
- **White Mold**: fluffy white mycelium and black sclerotia on stems

**Top candidates:**
- **Fusarium**: white pith, reddish-brown to dark brown rotted roots, brown vascular tissue — Fusarium reference (top-right panel) shows an almost identical configuration to the test image: plant held horizontally with dead black root system and split white-interior stem
- **Sudden Death Syndrome**: white pith (diagnostic), rotted roots, possible blue fungal growth — SDS reference shows rotted roots but also typically has foliar interveinal chlorosis

**Decision**: The Fusarium reference collage is the strongest visual match — particularly showing the same stem orientation held up with severely blackened/rotted roots and white interior pith. The complete destruction of lateral roots with cortical decay aligns with Fusarium root rot description ("reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots with poor nodulation and cortical decay").
